title: CALCULUS 2
body:
[[CALCULUS 1]] had two ideas, the [[Derivative]] and the [[Integral]], and one technique for each.
Calculus 2 is what happens when you take the second of those seriously. Half the course is
*machinery*: [[Integration Techniques]] for integrals that [[U-Substitution]] cannot touch,
[[Improper Integral]]s for regions that never end, and the geometric and physical quantities
([[Solids of Revolution]], [[Arc Length]], [[Applications of Integration]]) that turn out to be
integrals once you slice them thinly enough. The other half is the single best idea in the
sequence: **an infinite sum can be a number**, and once you believe that, a function can be an
infinite polynomial. That is [[Infinite Series]] into [[Power Series]] into [[Taylor Series]].

The through-line, if you keep one sentence: **Calc 1 approximated a curve by a line, Calc 2
approximates it by a polynomial of any degree you like, and then asks whether the approximation
survives being taken to infinity.** [[Linear Approximation]] is the degree-1 case and
[[Taylor Series]] is the same construction not stopped, which is why [[Convergence Tests]] is a
Tier 1 note in a course that looks like it is about integration: the whole series half of the
course is one question, does this sum settle down, asked with seven different tools.

For a CS degree the payoff is concrete. **[[Taylor Series]] is how `sin`, `exp`, and `ln`
are actually computed**, so the truncation error in a series is the same object as the rounding
error in [[Data representation]]. Convergence rate is why an algorithm that halves its error each
step beats one that shaves a fixed amount, the same comparison [[Time Complexity]] makes with
growth instead of decay. And a [[Probability Density Function]] in [[STATISTICS]] is legal only
because an [[Improper Integral]] over the whole line converges to $1$.

Two blocks of the official outline are introduced here and **owned by [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]**
(MATH 3200): differential equations, and the multivariable material. This parent says what Calc 2
does with them and links across rather than writing a second copy. The one exception is the
[[Double Integral]], which MRU teaches here; MATH 3200's [[Multiple Integration]] picks up triples.

## Topics

### Techniques of integration

- [[Integration Techniques]]: the selection table, and the note to read first. Which technique
  the *shape* of an integrand calls for, and the order to try them in
- [[Integration By Parts]]: $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$, the product rule run backwards. LIATE
  for choosing $u$, and the two cases (a power that dies, a loop that closes) where it terminates
- [[Integration By Trigonometric Substitution]]: the three triangles. Trade $x$ for a
  [[Trigonometric Function]] of $\theta$ so a Pythagorean identity kills the radical
- [[Integration By Partial Fractions]]: split a rational function into pieces whose antiderivatives
  are logs and arctangents, by the type of factor in the denominator
- [[Trigonometric Integrals]]: powers of sine, cosine, tangent, and secant, and the odd-power
  and half-angle strategies that reduce them
- [[Improper Integral]]: an infinite limit of integration or an infinite integrand. Defined as a
  [[Limit]] of proper integrals, and it either converges to a number or it does not exist

### Applications of integration

- [[Solids of Revolution]]: disks, washers, and cylindrical shells. Three formulas, one idea:
  slice, find the area of a slice, integrate
- [[Arc Length]]: the length of a curve, in Cartesian, parametric, and polar form. One note, three
  formulas, all the same [[Riemann Sum]] over tiny hypotenuses
- [[Applications of Integration]]: work, hydrostatic force, centroids, and centres of mass. The
  modelling pattern is identical every time and that is the thing to learn
- [[Double Integral]]: integrating over a region of the plane rather than an interval, volume under
  a surface, and where the area-under-a-curve picture stops being enough

### Sequences and series

- [[Sequence]]: an infinite list, its [[Limit]], and the bounded plus monotonic test that proves a
  limit exists without producing it
- [[Infinite Series]]: a sum defined as the limit of its partial sums, the geometric and $p$-series
  families, and the fact that the terms going to zero is not enough
- [[Convergence Tests]]: the selection table for the seven tests. The second Tier 1 note of the
  course, and the one exam questions are actually about
- [[Power Series]]: a series with an $x$ in it, its radius and interval of convergence, and the
  observation that inside that interval it behaves like a polynomial
- [[Taylor Series]]: the power series a function generates from its own derivatives at a point,
  which makes [[Linear Approximation]] the first two terms of something much longer
- [[Maclaurin Series]]: the Taylor series centred at $a = 0$, and the five expansions worth
  memorising

### Parametric equations and polar coordinates

- [[Parametric Equations]]: describe a curve by where a point is at time $t$ rather than by $y$ as
  a function of $x$, which lets a curve loop, cross itself, and have vertical tangents
- [[Polar Coordinates]]: locate a point by distance and angle. Conversion both ways, graphing
  $r = f(\theta)$, and area as a sum of thin circular sectors rather than thin rectangles

### Differential equations (introduced here, owned by MATH 3200)

Calc 2 meets [[Differential Equations]] as an application of integration: separation of variables
is "get the $y$s on one side and integrate both", the integrating factor handles linear
first-order equations, and second-order homogeneous equations reduce to the roots of a
characteristic polynomial. [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] owns all of it, including
[[Homogeneous ODE]], [[Non-Homogeneous ODE]], [[Undetermined Coefficients]], and [[Cauchy-Euler]].
The link back to this course: **an ODE is solved by integrating, so every technique above is a
prerequisite**, and [[Power Series]] solutions are the method of last resort when none of them work.

### Multivariable calculus (introduced here, owned by MATH 3200)

The last block puts more than one variable in and stops. What Calc 2 says: a function of two
variables is a surface, a [[Partial Derivative]] is the ordinary derivative with the other
variables held constant, the [[Gradient]] collects them into a vector pointing uphill, and the
[[Multivariable Chain Rule]] is [[Chain Rule]] summed over every path a dependence can take.
[[Multivariable Calculus]] and [[Vector Calculus]] in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] take it properly.

## Core Facts to Know

- **The four techniques, in the order to try them**: substitution first (it is Calc 1's and it is
  cheapest), then parts, then partial fractions if the integrand is rational, then trig
  substitution if there is a radical of the form $\sqrt{a^2 \pm x^2}$ or $\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}$.
- $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$. Choose $u$ so that $du$ is *simpler*: **LIATE** (logarithmic,
  inverse trig, algebraic, trigonometric, exponential) is the priority order for $u$.
- Parts terminates in exactly two ways: the algebraic factor differentiates down to zero
  ($\int x^2 e^x dx$, three rounds), or the original integral reappears and you solve for it
  algebraically ($\int e^x \sin x\,dx$, two rounds). If neither happens, the choice of $u$ was wrong.
- $\int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - x + C$ is parts with $dv = dx$. The trick is that $u$ can be the
  whole integrand.
- Partial fractions needs the degree of the numerator **below** the degree of the denominator.
  Otherwise divide first. A repeated linear factor $(x-a)^k$ gets $k$ terms, one for each power;
  an irreducible quadratic gets a $\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+bx+c}$ numerator, not a constant.
- The three trig substitutions: $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ takes $x = a\sin\theta$, $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ takes
  $x = a\tan\theta$, $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$ takes $x = a\sec\theta$. Each one turns the radical into
  $a\cos\theta$, $a\sec\theta$, or $a\tan\theta$ by one Pythagorean identity. **Draw the triangle**
  to convert back.
- An [[Improper Integral]] is *defined* as a limit: $\int_a^\infty f = \lim_{t\to\infty}\int_a^t f$.
  It is not "plug in infinity". If the limit does not exist, the integral **diverges** and there is
  no answer to give.
- $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^p}$ converges **iff $p > 1$**. Near zero it is the other way:
  $\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{x^p}$ converges iff $p < 1$. Both are worth knowing cold, since they are the
  comparison every other improper integral is judged against.
- Disk/washer integrates **perpendicular** to the axis of revolution, shells integrate **parallel**
  to it. Pick whichever avoids solving the curve for the other variable. Shell volume element:
  $2\pi(\text{radius})(\text{height})\,dx$.
- Arc length is $\int \sqrt{1 + (f'(x))^2}\,dx$ in Cartesian,
  $\int \sqrt{(dx/dt)^2 + (dy/dt)^2}\,dt$ parametric, $\int \sqrt{r^2 + (dr/d\theta)^2}\,d\theta$
  polar. All three are $\int \sqrt{dx^2+dy^2}$ with different things factored out.
- Work is $\int F(x)\,dx$, and the whole difficulty of the physical applications is deciding what
  is varying with the slice variable: the force, the distance moved, or the density.
- A [[Sequence]] is a function on the integers and converges iff its terms approach a single value.
  A [[Infinite Series|series]] is the sequence of its **partial sums**, and converges iff *that*
  sequence converges. Confusing the two is the most common error in the block.
- **The $n$th term test is only a divergence test.** If $a_n \not\to 0$ the series diverges; if
  $a_n \to 0$ it tells you **nothing**. The harmonic series $\sum 1/n$ has terms going to zero and
  diverges anyway, which is the counterexample the whole course hangs on.
- Geometric series: $\sum_{n=0}^\infty ar^n$ converges iff $|r| < 1$, to $\frac{a}{1-r}$. It is the
  only common series whose **sum** you can write down, not merely test.
- $p$-series: $\sum \frac{1}{n^p}$ converges iff $p > 1$. Same threshold as the improper integral,
  and that is not a coincidence: the integral test is the proof.
- **Ratio test for factorials and $n$th powers, root test for $n$th powers, comparison for
  rational-looking terms, alternating series test when signs alternate.** $L < 1$ converges,
  $L > 1$ diverges, $L = 1$ means the test failed and you need a different one.
- **Absolute convergence implies convergence, not the reverse.** $\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$ converges
  conditionally: rearranging its terms can make it sum to anything you like, which is the reason
  the distinction is not pedantry.
- A [[Power Series]] converges on an interval centred at $a$, always: at $a$ only, on all of
  $\mathbb{R}$, or on a radius $R$ where the ratio test gives $R$ and **the two endpoints have to be
  checked separately by hand**.
- $f(x) = \sum \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n$. Every coefficient is a derivative at one point,
  which is the surprising claim: the behaviour of an analytic function everywhere is encoded in
  its derivatives at a single point.
- The five [[Maclaurin Series]] to know:
  $e^x = \sum \frac{x^n}{n!}$, $\sin x = \sum \frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}$,
  $\cos x = \sum \frac{(-1)^n x^{2n}}{(2n)!}$, $\frac{1}{1-x} = \sum x^n$ for $|x|<1$, and
  $\ln(1+x) = \sum \frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^n}{n}$. Everything else is built from these by substituting,
  differentiating, integrating, or multiplying.
- **Truncating a Taylor series is what a computer does to evaluate $\sin x$**, and the alternating
  series error bound (the error is smaller than the first omitted term) is what tells it when to
  stop.
- Parametric: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$, and the second derivative is
  $\frac{d}{dt}\!\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) \big/ \frac{dx}{dt}$, **not** $\frac{d^2y/dt^2}{d^2x/dt^2}$.
- Polar conversion: $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, $r^2 = x^2+y^2$,
  $\tan\theta = y/x$ **with the quadrant checked**. Identical formulas to [[Polar Form]] in
  [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]], applied to the plane rather than to $\mathbb{C}$.
- Polar area is $\frac{1}{2}\int r^2\,d\theta$, sectors rather than rectangles. The $\frac12 r^2$
  is the area of a circular wedge, and forgetting the $\frac12$ is the standard slip.

## Related courses

- [[CALCULUS 1]] (MATH 1200) is the prerequisite and the handoff is exact. Calc 1 stops at
  [[U-Substitution]], so [[Integration Techniques]] picks up from there; [[Taylor Series]] is
  [[Linear Approximation]] continued past the first term; and every convergence question in
  [[Infinite Series]] is a [[Limit]] question. [[Riemann Sum]] is the construction every
  application in this course re-runs with a different slice.
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] (MATH 3200) is the sequel and owns the two blocks this course only
  introduces: [[Differential Equations]] and the multivariable material
  ([[Partial Derivative]], [[Gradient]], [[Multivariable Chain Rule]], [[Multivariable Calculus]]).
  [[Double Integral]] here, [[Multiple Integration]] there.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234): a [[Probability Density Function]] is normalised by an
  [[Improper Integral]] over an infinite domain, the exponential and gamma densities are evaluated
  by [[Integration By Parts]], and [[Average Value]] is a definite integral. The convergence
  questions are this course's, the interpretation is that one's.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) is the other way to write a function as an infinite
  sum. [[Taylor Series]] uses powers of $(x-a)$ and is local; [[Fourier Series]] uses sines and
  cosines and is global. Both are "expand in a basis", which is what [[Orthogonal Functions]]
  makes precise, and the coefficients there are integrals evaluated by the techniques here.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203): [[Polar Form]] does modulus and argument for a complex number
  with the same conversion formulas [[Polar Coordinates]] uses for a point in the plane. Two notes,
  one trigonometry; each says what it is not.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303): [[Vector Norm]] is the discrete version of the
  arc length and $L^2$ integrals here, and [[Wavelet Transform]] is a basis expansion with the
  same convergence bookkeeping.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655): [[Taylor Series]] truncation is how transcendental
  functions get computed at all, and the error left over is the same size as the representation
  error in [[Data representation]].
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]]: [[Gradient Descent]] converges or does not for the same reason a
  [[Sequence]] does, and "converges linearly" versus "converges quadratically" is a statement about
  the ratio of successive errors, which is the ratio test wearing a different hat.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631): the geometric series is where
  $\sum_{i=0}^{\log n} \frac{n}{2^i} = O(n)$ comes from, which is why [[Merge Sort]]'s
  merge work and [[Recursion|recursive]] halving analyses land where they do.
